power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: A positive delirium screen should trigger timely assessment and care, but the initial bedside response is not always clearly defined.
ACE-T (Acute Triggers / Patient Experience / Treatments) is a nurse-led tool (https://www.theace-t.com/) that sets out initial care actions and supports documentation and team communication.
text.formatted: ACE-T (Acute Triggers / Patient Experience / Treatments) is a nurse-led tool (<ref type="url" target="https://www.theace-t.com/">www.theace-t.com</ref>) that sets out initial care actions and supports documentation and team communication.

text.text: Delirium care involves three core elements: detection, treatment, and prevention. [1] [2] [3] [4] Standard approaches for detection and prevention are well established in the literature. [5] [6] [7] [8] By contrast, delirium treatment is much less well defined. 1, 9 Across guidelines and other sources, approaches to delirium treatment commonly describe a package of multiple actions including, for example, identifying and addressing triggers, managing symptoms, and promoting recovery. 2, 3, [10] [11] [12] [13] Yet these approaches show substantial variations in content and operationalization.
text.formatted: Delirium care involves three core elements: detection, treatment, and prevention. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> Standard approaches for detection and prevention are well established in the literature. <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> By contrast, delirium treatment is much less well defined. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> Across guidelines and other sources, approaches to delirium treatment commonly describe a package of multiple actions including, for example, identifying and addressing triggers, managing symptoms, and promoting recovery. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> Yet these approaches show substantial variations in content and operationalization.

text.text: In guidelines, delirium treatment has a range of labels, including 'multicomponent non-pharmacological interventions', a 'multicomponent program', 'non-drug strategies', and 'established pathways of good care'.
The content ranges from two brief recommendations to a 15-component program. 2, 3, [10] [11] [12] [13] Most guidelines do not define which professional groups are responsible for what actions.
text.formatted: The content ranges from two brief recommendations to a 15-component program. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> Most guidelines do not define which professional groups are responsible for what actions.

text.text: Exceptions are the American Psychiatric Association 2025 guideline, 12 which notes that nurses "deliver or assure delivery" of most non-pharmacological interventions, and the German guideline 13 which places the acute etiological work-up at specialist-physician level and allocates non-pharmacological interventions to nursing, occupational therapy and physiotherapy by problem domain.
text.formatted: Exceptions are the American Psychiatric Association 2025 guideline, <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> which notes that nurses "deliver or assure delivery" of most non-pharmacological interventions, and the German guideline <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> which places the acute etiological work-up at specialist-physician level and allocates non-pharmacological interventions to nursing, occupational therapy and physiotherapy by problem domain.

text.text: Even these exceptions are partial: neither defines the sequence or timing of actions required of nurses in the hours immediately after a positive screen.

Outside guidelines, delirium treatment is described in research studies, book chapters, order sets, and clinical pathways. [14] [15] [16] As with guidelines, these sources vary considerably in sequence, timing, role of different disciplines (which is often not specified), and documentation.
text.formatted: Outside guidelines, delirium treatment is described in research studies, book chapters, order sets, and clinical pathways. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[16]</ref> As with guidelines, these sources vary considerably in sequence, timing, role of different disciplines (which is often not specified), and documentation.

text.text: A consequence of this lack of standardization is that clinical teams vary substantially in how they respond after a positive delirium screen.

Studies show variation and deficiencies in identifying modifiable triggers, assessing and managing patient distress, and communicating the diagnosis to patients and families. [17] [18] [19] [20] [21] One potentially useful term for the package of actions involved in treatment is 'multidomain' delirium treatment. 1 The term avoids the misleading division of clinical delirium treatment into distinct 'nonpharmacological' and 'pharmacological' elements.
text.formatted: Studies show variation and deficiencies in identifying modifiable triggers, assessing and managing patient distress, and communicating the diagnosis to patients and families. <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[21]</ref> One potentially useful term for the package of actions involved in treatment is 'multidomain' delirium treatment. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> The term avoids the misleading division of clinical delirium treatment into distinct 'nonpharmacological' and 'pharmacological' elements.

text.text: This is important because guidelines advise against giving psychotropic drugs routinely, but they do permit brief, targeted use if necessary for intractable distress or safety considerations. 2, 3, [10] [11] [12] [13] This means that the use of drugs is simply one optional tool in a wider set of possible actions, not an implied treatment category of its own.
text.formatted: This is important because guidelines advise against giving psychotropic drugs routinely, but they do permit brief, targeted use if necessary for intractable distress or safety considerations. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> This means that the use of drugs is simply one optional tool in a wider set of possible actions, not an implied treatment category of its own.

text.text: 'Multidomain' also separates this package-based approach from single-intervention strategies, such as drug-based or music-based interventions.
Here we use the term multidomain to describe mainstream delirium treatment as used in routine clinical care.

Although the roles of the healthcare team overlap, it is reasonable for different disciplines to focus on the aspects of delirium treatment best suited to each, as stated in the American and German guidelines, and in some published studies. 12, 13, [22] [23] [24] [25] [26] In many healthcare systems, nurses are the main group carrying out delirium screening, meaning that they are in the ideal position to respond as soon as a screen is positive.
text.formatted: Although the roles of the healthcare team overlap, it is reasonable for different disciplines to focus on the aspects of delirium treatment best suited to each, as stated in the American and German guidelines, and in some published studies. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[22]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[23]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[24]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[25]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[26]</ref> In many healthcare systems, nurses are the main group carrying out delirium screening, meaning that they are in the ideal position to respond as soon as a screen is positive.

text.text: Nurses also have a central role in the ongoing care of patients with delirium: managing interventions, monitoring distress, communicating with families, and keeping patients safe.
Given the urgency of delirium treatment and the central role of nurses in detection and care, a practical nurse-focused tool is needed to guide the first steps after a positive screen.
Such a tool could help standardize these first steps, alongside the complementary medical and other roles in delirium care.

Additionally, several studies have identified gaps in escalation and clinical action following a positive delirium screen, [27] [28] [29] [30] and nurses are well placed to take rapid action and help initiate involvement of other team members.
text.formatted: Additionally, several studies have identified gaps in escalation and clinical action following a positive delirium screen, <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[27]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[28]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[29]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[30]</ref> and nurses are well placed to take rapid action and help initiate involvement of other team members.

text.text: Here we describe the development and preliminary piloting of the ACE-T tool (ACute Triggers / patient Experience / Treatments).
This is a brief nurse-led multidomain delirium treatment tool intended to standardize initial bedside nursing actions following a positive delirium screen.

Our aims were: (1) to assess the usability and perceived utility of the tool among multidisciplinary clinical staff; (2) to describe how nurse-led delirium-care actions were documented after a positive screen; and (3) to identify implementation and measurement lessons for a future, more definitive evaluation.

We used a staged, multicenter developmental pilot design comprising development of a provisional ACE-T tool; a pre-introduction staff survey and revision; and site-led pilot use with a descriptive before-andafter review of clinical documentation.
The work took place at Stanford Hospital (Stanford, USA), AGAPLESION Markus Krankenhaus (Frankfurt, Germany), and the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh (Edinburgh, UK).
Baseline record-review data were collected in summer 2025 and post-introduction data in autumn and winter 2025-2026.
The study assessed staff perceptions, documentation patterns, and measurement issues; it was not designed to estimate clinical effectiveness.

AM, MH, AC and JT iteratively drafted the provisional tool drawing from published delirium guidelines and clinical care standards, 2, 3, 11 the structure and content of the multidisciplinary Triggers, Investigations, Management and Engagement (TIME) bundle, 2 and our clinical experience.
text.formatted: AM, MH, AC and JT iteratively drafted the provisional tool drawing from published delirium guidelines and clinical care standards, <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> the structure and content of the multidisciplinary Triggers, Investigations, Management and Engagement (TIME) bundle, <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> and our clinical experience.

text.text: The ACE-T (https://www.theace-t.com/) was developed to support nurse-led action in the first hours after a positive delirium screen or recognition of suspected delirium.
text.formatted: The ACE-T (<ref type="url" target="https://www.theace-t.com/">www.theace-t.com</ref>) was developed to support nurse-led action in the first hours after a positive delirium screen or recognition of suspected delirium.

text.text: The nursing focus was informed by evidence of deficiencies in post-screen clinical responses and by nurses' key role in the early assessment, escalation and ongoing care of patients with delirium. 18, 20, 27, 29, 31, 32 The ACE-T organizes actions into the three domains of (1) ACute triggers, (2) patient Experience, and (3) Treatment and communication.
text.formatted: The nursing focus was informed by evidence of deficiencies in post-screen clinical responses and by nurses' key role in the early assessment, escalation and ongoing care of patients with delirium. <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">29,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">31,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">32</ref> The ACE-T organizes actions into the three domains of (1) ACute triggers, (2) patient Experience, and (3) Treatment and communication.

text.text: These domains were chosen to prioritize early nursing actions while keeping the tool pragmatic.

The ACE-T prompts consideration of observations, review of whether clinically indicated investigations and medication review have occurred, assessment of distress (with the option of using a brief 4-point tool called the Quick Distress Assessment Tool (QDAT, Table 1)) 21 and the care environment, documentation of delirium, and communication with the clinical team and family.
text.formatted: The ACE-T prompts consideration of observations, review of whether clinically indicated investigations and medication review have occurred, assessment of distress (with the option of using a brief 4-point tool called the Quick Distress Assessment Tool (QDAT, Table <ref type="table">1</ref>)) <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">21</ref> and the care environment, documentation of delirium, and communication with the clinical team and family.

text.text: It does not require nurses to diagnose the cause or order investigations outside local policy, and it does not replace wider multidisciplinary care; the communication domain supports team involvement.
Early drafts underwent revisions following feedback from nurses and physician colleagues to refine layout and content.

Before clinical use, local investigators invited a convenience sample of nurses, physicians, physician associates or assistants, and nurse practitioners to review the provisional tool and complete an anonymous paper questionnaire (Supplement 1).
It recorded professional group and delirium-care experience.
Four five-level items assessed ease of understanding and use, clarity, and perceived helpfulness for guiding and improving care.
A yes/no item with free text asked whether any section was unclear or difficult, and an open question invited suggested changes.
Ratings reflected perceived rather than observed usability.
Participation was voluntary, and return indicated consent.
The project group reviewed the ratings and comments and revised the content and layout.

The revised version retained the three domains, clarified nursing actions and medical escalation, simplified Acute Triggers, and expanded prompts about distress, reorientation, sensory aids, carers, and safety.

Following feedback concerning various timescales for completion, it set a target of 4 hours from the positive screen for completing, initiating, or escalating applicable actions; urgent concerns required immediate action.
The questionnaire is provided in Supplement 1, and the revised pilot version is shown in Table 1.
text.formatted: The questionnaire is provided in Supplement 1, and the revised pilot version is shown in Table <ref type="table">1</ref>.

text.text: Each site introduced ACE-T through existing clinical teams without a shared training package or standardized procedure (Table 2).
text.formatted: Each site introduced ACE-T through existing clinical teams without a shared training package or standardized procedure (Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: At Stanford, the geriatric Clinical Nurse Specialist introduced the paper tool on the Acute Care for Elders unit after a positive Confusion Assessment Method screen.
Edinburgh used a paper tool in geriatric medicine wards.
In Frankfurt, the medical ward delirium team used ACE-T after a positive 4AT and recorded actions electronically.
We did not assess uptake, fidelity, or completion within 4 hours.
Local reviewers identified 10 records before and 10 after introduction at each site (60 records).
Eligible records contained a positive delirium screen or documented clinical diagnosis; screening instruments followed routine local practice.
Case identification was not standardized or random, and samples were not intended to represent all eligible admissions.
Post-introduction samples in Edinburgh and Stanford came from geriatric units, whereas baseline samples included more general medical wards.
The index event was the earliest positive qualifying screen or, if none was recorded, the earliest explicit clinical documentation of delirium.
A structured extraction form (Supplement 2) recorded age, sex, ward, time from admission to the index event, and documentation of prespecified care actions during the next 48 hours.
These covered distress, pain, physiological contributors, delirium documentation, communication, written information, and patient-centered actions.
Completed ACE-T forms counted as post-introduction documentation where available.
The review described documentation, not adherence to the 4-hour target or all bedside care.
Reviewers were clinicians familiar with delirium care at their site and used locally available records.
German baseline data came from delirium-team records rather than the full ward record; an absent item therefore meant it was not documented by that team, not that ward staff had not completed it.
Reviewers knew the study phase, and we did not test inter-rater reliability.
We summarized survey items as frequencies and percentages, using available responses as denominators with no imputation; positive ratings combined the two highest categories.
We grouped free text pragmatically into recurring categories to guide revision rather than undertaking formal qualitative analysis.
We summarized age as mean (standard deviation), admission-to-index time as median, and categorical variables as counts and percentages.
Care-action counts and proportions were reported by site and phase, excluding missing or not-applicable entries.
We did not pool effects or perform hypothesis tests because samples were small and non-random and sites differed in ward mix and record sources.

At Stanford, the institutional review board determined that the project did not constitute human subjects research and that no further IRB review was required (protocol 79545, "What to do about a positive delirium screen").
At Frankfurt, the institutional review board of the state of Hesse approved the use of retrospectively collected data (2026-4463-evBO).
The Edinburgh component was an approved service evaluation project under local quality improvement governance.
Survey responses were anonymous.
Sites removed direct patient identifiers, assigned study codes, and collated only de-identified data.
The structured survey was completed by 53 multidisciplinary staff (26 nurses, 19 physicians and 8 advanced practice providers).

Respondents rated the ACE-T favorably overall: 75% (39/52) rated it as easy or very easy to use, 77% (41/53) rated its instructions and steps as clear or very clear, 70% (37/53) rated it as very or extremely helpful for nursing assessment and management, and 71% (37/52) rated it as very or extremely helpful for improving their current approach to delirium care.
Nevertheless, 40% (21/52) identified a section that was unclear or difficult, and 22 respondents provided free-text suggestions.

Recurring suggestions were to distinguish nursing from medical actions more clearly, especially within Acute Triggers; simplify that section for a busy workflow; integrate ACE-T with existing documentation to avoid duplication; expand person-centered strategies within Patient Experience; and phrase items as questions or instructions.

Specific areas of uncertainty included medication review (5/22, 23%), diagnostic work-up and laboratory-ordering boundaries (5/22, 23%), Acute Triggers (4/22, 18%), layout (4/22, 18%), and NEWS2 or QDAT (3/22, 14%).
These findings informed the revisions described in the Methods.
Sixty records were reviewed (30 before and 30 after introduction; 10 per site in each phase).

Mean age was similar (pre-introduction 86.2 years [SD 6.7; n=29 with age recorded] and post-introduction 85.9 years [SD 6.7; n=30]), whereas the proportion of male patients differed (63% and 43%, respectively).
Median time from admission to the index event was 1 day in both phases.
Ward mix changed substantially: 70% of pre-introduction records came from general medical wards and 3% from geriatric wards, compared with 23% and 67%, respectively, after introduction.
At the UK and US sites, all postintroduction records came from geriatric units.
Findings are therefore reported as site-level descriptive counts rather than pooled before-and-after comparisons.
The most consistent site-level pattern concerned documentation of delirium or suspected delirium (Table 3).

The ACE-T addresses a practical gap between detecting delirium and initiating a coordinated response.
In this pilot, staff from several disciplines generally found the tool clear, usable and helpful, and their feedback informed changes to scope, workflow and person-centered content.
Across all three sites, the record review found that delirium or suspected delirium and communication with the medical team were documented more often after introduction.
The same delirium-specific documentation pattern was seen across the three systems.

Detection alone does not ensure that delirium is documented or escalated, and previous studies describe the same postscreen gap. 20, 29, [31] [32] [33] [34] The ACE-T offers a structured way to make the expected initial response explicit and more visible within the wider multidisciplinary pathway.

text.text: Testing at three sites showed the need for local adaptation, and a shared framework may support a more consistent and coordinated response.
The ACE-T is an initial-response prompt focused on key nursing elements of delirium treatment.
It is not a diagnostic instrument or complete treatment pathway.

It prompts nurses to consider appropriate comfort, observation, assessment and person-centered measures; make possible triggers visible; document suspected delirium; communicate with the team and escalate concerns according to local policy.

This is consistent with guidance recommending rapid assessment, management of acute triggers and mitigation of other contributors (such as sensory impairments), supportive care, communication and multidisciplinary management. 2, 3, [10] [11] [12] [13] Diagnosis, prescribing and definitive treatment remain multidisciplinary and scope-dependent.
text.formatted: This is consistent with guidance recommending rapid assessment, management of acute triggers and mitigation of other contributors (such as sensory impairments), supportive care, communication and multidisciplinary management. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> Diagnosis, prescribing and definitive treatment remain multidisciplinary and scope-dependent.

text.text: The 4-hour interval was a pragmatic completion target, not a known safety threshold.
Urgent concerns require immediate action, and team members should work in parallel, using clinical judgement depending on the clinical situation.
In Edinburgh, investigators considered the tool's explicit nursing focus and simple, stepwise format important for local engagement and implementation.
The staged development was a strength.

Feedback informed revision before pilot use, and testing in three systems identified contextual differences in professional scope, terminology, workflow and documentation that a single-site study might have missed.
Current guidance on complex interventions similarly emphasizes context, stakeholder perspectives and iterative refinement. 35 This preliminary study has limitations.
text.formatted: Current guidance on complex interventions similarly emphasizes context, stakeholder perspectives and iterative refinement. <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">35</ref> This preliminary study has limitations.

text.text: Completed ACE-T forms counted as post-introduction documentation, so the study could not distinguish changes in bedside care from changes in recording.
The 48-hour window did not test completion within 4 hours.
German baseline data came from deliriumteam records, while ward mix changed between phases in the UK and USA.
Eligible-case denominators, reach, uptake and fidelity were not measured consistently; confounding and contextual differences limit direct comparisons and generalizability.
Other limitations include small convenience samples, non-random case selection, heterogeneous triggers, unblinded review, no inter-rater reliability testing and possible concurrent influences.
The preuse questionnaire was unvalidated, 26 of 53 respondents were nurses, and observed usability was not assessed.
Factors supporting local engagement were not formally evaluated.
Patients and family carers were not involved in initial development.
The communication item did not establish the recipient, content or quality of information.
Safety outcomes, unintended consequences, repeat use and staff burden were not assessed.

ACE-T also depends on reliable upstream detection, which remains variable in routine practice. 8, 18 A prospective feasibility study should co-design the implementation of the tool with bedside nurses, patients and carers; examine how the ACE-T integrates with the work of other disciplines; formally assess content validity and usability; and recruit consecutive eligible cases.

text.text: Measures should distinguish implementation from clinical effects and include reach, adoption, 4-hour completion, fidelity, staff burden, acceptability, patient and carer communication, and unintended consequences. 36 Electronic integration should be tested, including whether it reduces duplicate recording without adding alert or documentation burden.

text.text: Establishing feasibility and measurement methods would provide a basis for evaluating clinical effectiveness.
The ACE-T is a promising, practical tool for the initial nursing response to delirium.
Its stepwise format offers a straightforward starting point for teams seeking to make these first steps clearer and more consistent in routine care.
Future work will help assess its value in clinical practice.
